review_text_raw:
Hacknet is an absolute gem of a game. 

[b]TLDR: [/b]While people already familiar with using *nix or general programing principles may find this game not too deep or challenging, it offers a well thought out narrative, with fun game mechanics and excels at teaching you about computer essentials without you even realizing it. 


[b]More thoughts:[/b] 

While this game isn't perfect, I would still reccomend it to anyone who has even a remote interest in computers. Even if you only want to feel like a hacker in a movie, that game gives you that feeling. If you want to learn more about the general concepts of computer-, program-, and network-architecture, this game is a great launching-point, before you start reading more "serious" or conventional literature on the subject. 

Now, the mechanics are pretty straight-forward. You gain various programs through completing quests, which, in turn, can be used to bypass more complex security. You also gain the ability to run commands through other computers, allowing you, for example, to pretty much emulate a DDOS attack. Timing is also important, so be ready to type "dc" + [enter] if you're being tracked. AAAAAAAAANNNNNNDDDDDD............

.....
.....
.....

that's pretty much it when it comes to mechanics. The rest is working your way through systems full of mostly text-files, a lot of them taken from bash.org (hilarious quotes from internet chats, NSFW, but great!), and a lot of fun easter-eggs for nerds and fans of "hacker-culture" as it has been created by Hollywood. There even are multiple references to the movie "Hackers", a must see in my opinion. ;)

Now, the mechanics got old after not too long (a good 8 hours), mainly due to you unlocking a lot of the tools that you need pretty quickly. I'll talk more about overall gameplay features in just a moment. 

The narrative is fun, well paced, and interwoven well with the gameplay mechanics. I won't spoil anything, just watch the trailer and you get the general premise. 

The overall game is simplified, to allow people without prior experience to enjoy it, but encourages experimentation and exploration of what you can do, giving you plenty of examples and hints along the way to teach you, without you even realizing it, a lot about how your system works. Absolutely amazing!

Concerning the lack of gameplay features, the dev is amazing. Yup, one dev. And he's already said that he wants to implement multiplayer. If that happens, this will become one of the best games out there. Period. Plus he wants to continue to push content for the game. Not to mention, that the community as a whole is awesome and really suportive for newcomers. 

In its current state, it's well worth the price its asking for. As the dev continues to push more content, the game will continue to expand and improve. 

Please support this game, as its honestly trying to be different and fun, without a lot of the backstabbing and abusive tactics emplyed by all too many triple AAA studios/publishers. I can guarantee, you'll have a blast playing this!

Edit 2016: what I've said before still applies. I would just like to point towards the roadmap the dev has for 2016, which includes multiplayer and steam-workshop integration for custom missions throughout various points this year. http://steamcommunity.com/games/365450/announcements/detail/955130645658936382 

****DISCLAIMER:****
 WIll not actually refund any purchases if you are somehow not pleased with the overall game. 
Mouse and Mechanical Keyboard sold seperatly.
Batteries not included.

review_text_raw:
This is gonna be a lengthy review. I'll add a TL;DR at the bottom.

When I first went to view the page for this game, there were many questions that began flooding my mind. And now that I've played the game almost to its entirety, I think that I can answer most of these questions that interested consumers passing by may have. This game was a real treat, and I think that it deserves more attention than it's received.


[h1] Is Hacknet realistic? [/h1]

If you mean "realistic" as in "Is this game close to hacking in real life?" then the answer is no. This game is not realistic because it is fun and doesn't make you paranoid. You are in possession of a bunch of hacking tools that put up the kinds of graphics you'd expect to be running on computers in a 90's hacker film, and the way these tools work is by executing them and waiting for the flashy hacking graphics to stop flashing so that you can run another flashy hacker tool until you gain administrative system access. Granted, it's more complex than that, which is why this game is really enjoyable, but you're not going to be writing complex algorithms to overload proxy servers and bypass tracing measures. That's what the 90's tools are for.

That being said, this may be as close as gaming will ever come to realistic hacking. Because anything that tries to be precicely like real hacking that doesn't give you fancy hacker programs probably isn't going to be a very fun game. And this, again, is a fun game. The entire game takes place on a computer's operating system, and every hack you perform is done through this system. In addition, the commands you use are based on real UNIX commands, even if the commands are typically used to activate the previously-mentioned hacking programs. It's certainly more realistic than games where you push a button and your character goes [i]"I'm in" [/i] like Watch_Dogs and Quadrilateral Cowboy (That isn't to say that they're bad games, just that they're not trying to be realistic hacking simulations which, again, isn't necessarily a bad thing).


[h1] Is this game immersive? Will I feel like a hacker even if I'm not performing real hacks? [/h1]

Oh, yes. If you want to feel like the genius hacker that always appears in Hollywood films but rarely gets any time for actual character development, then this game is for you. The presentation of this game is great, and it really helps to sell that feeling of accomplishment that you get when you pull off a successful job. After about 30 minutes in, I had to re-check the steam store to make sure that I wasn't accessing a multiplayer hacking simulator. But nope, I was even able to play this game in airplane mode. As the store page mentions, there are very few things that break the immersion by being obvious parts of a video game. To complete a job, you email the client explaining that you've finished. To acquire a new tool, you have to copy said tool to your home computer from its rightful owner. 

And this immersive presentation goes a long way in the overall experience. I know that not everybody responds the same way, but I found certain parts to incite genuine emotion in a way that few other games have managed to pull off. Like when you're given the option to accept a job in which [spoiler]you have to euthanize a dying man by hacking his pacemaker [/spoiler], or when [spoiler]you run "OpenCDtray" on your own system and your real computer's disc tray opens and may potentially scare the hell out of you[/spoiler]. So even if you're using overpowered tools to open systems that nobody bothers to check, you'll probably still feel really good doing so.


[h1] Do I need to know coding or hacking in order to understand this game? [/h1]

No, you don't. The tutorial explains everything pretty well, and it makes sure that you understand how the systems work before even thinking about letting you out into the hacking world. No coding is required (I'm not even sure if coding algorithms is possible with the interface), and most of the game's difficulty comes with memorizing the commands and executing them at the appropriate times. That being said, if you don't know a whole lot about computers, the most difficult task will probably be [spoiler] getting your interface back after being locked to terminal mode by another hacker [/spoiler]. But if you experiment enough, then you'll ususally find the solutions to most of the challenges, and there are plenty of walkthroughs and tips out there if you end up getting desperate. But I was able to finish the game with little prior programming experience. If you know how to navigate a computer's interface or have downloaded and fixed mods on to other games, then you'll probably be fine with this game. Just, you know, don't delete important files or screw up on a trace aversion. I don't know if this game prevents you from screwing yourself over, and everybody's too scared to find out.


[h1] Is the game worth ten bucks? [/h1]

Yeah, I'd say so. You'll probably get around 10 hours out of it if you're doing the main story without any outside assitance, 14-15 hours if you're also doing the labrynths DLC. I'd say that it's not everybody's cup of tea; surely, your relative who spends all day exclusively playing [i] Fortnite [/i] would probably get turned off by this, but odds are you're at least mildly interested in this game if you're reading this review right now, considering that this game gets talked about as much as what brand of toilet paper you prefer when you're finished up on the toilet. So yeah, I'd recommend this game to anybody reading this review.


[h1] Oh, boy. It's one of those games that tries to sell its soundtrack as DLC. Is it good enough to warrant a purchase? [/h1]

I was honestly surprised by this game's soundtrack. Again, I understand that everybody has different tastes in music, but I found this particular OST track good to write and do homework to. It felt really good to listen to in-game while hacking servers and computers. The music is used as sort of an indicator on what part of the game you're currently at, and when the song changes, you know you're probably making progress. I found that [spoiler] Roller Mobster by Carpenter Brut [/spoiler] fit this game better than it did for HM2. That being said, I haven't purchased the soundtrack since most of it is available on YouTube anyways. And yes, it's ten dollars. Fifteen dollars for the main game and DLC soundtrack. So while I'll admit that the soundtrack is pretty good, I'd only spend the extra fifteen bucks if you like having the songs directly at your fingertips at all times.


[h1] TL;DR [/h1]

This is a great game that may be as close to realistic hacking as gaming will come while still remaining enjoyable. The presentation and aeshetic really add a lot to it, and you don't need to be experienced with programming or hacking in order to complete it. It's worth the money and gives around 10 hours of playtime assuming you don't mess up massively and have to start a new game. I'm gonna give this a thumbs up, and I wish it came out later so that I could put it in my favorite 2018 games list.

review_text_raw:
Many will claim that this is like playing the next version of Uplink since it is the most realistic hacking type game since Uplink was released. A very cult genre I think with very few games making a significant mark. I cannot claim to have played that classic so I will have to describe this entertaining game called Hacknet without any past comparisons. I will say that the reason it is compared though is because it takes the hacking seriously and isn't just some casual hacking game for the masses. 

Hacknet has almost no graphics (Maybe about 5 image files in the entire game), it has no video. It is only you looking at a computer screen full of numbers and files. You are a hacker, not Rambo, or James Bond, or Batman. You don't shoot at criminals and punch clowns in the face to save the day. You are a hacker that has found yourself in the middle of some hacking factions that may have stumbled into something big. You get some simple clues at the start that something is going on, but as you delve deeper into the hacking world, get recruited by more skillful hacking groups, and find more mysterious actions going on in your hacking exploits you will get asked to help find out what happened to a popular hacker that has gone missing. Just like everything in the hacking community, all useful information is hidden on systems which need to be hacked into. While looking for that information you will uncover many more secrets as you figure out exactly what happened. A final ending that could be considered a "shock". Very intriguing storyline and way to tell a story all through computer documents, e-mails, IRC chats, etc. 

While the tutorials, and the game itself is friendly to those who have no experience entering command lines, or hacking at all, it may not exactly be for the most casual of gamers. If you are a VERY slow typist you may have some issues when it comes to hacking into computers here in the time frames that are allowed. They have made it easier for you by allowing you to hit "TAB" in certain places to have the game auto-complete command lines if there is nothing else that has the exact same characters and you are in the proper place to do so, however. It absolutely helps to have some typing speed, or at least the knowledge of where all the keys on the keyboard are without having to search them out all the time though. You will have issues if you are THAT slow.  

You are tasked with finding various tools to run .exe files allowing you to open up ports on the computers you hack before running a PortHack program to get access to its files. Some computers early on are very easy to hack with only having to open 1-2 ports, but as you find more tools you may have to open as many as 5 ports, break through a firewall, and get through a proxy all on the same PC while avoiding a tracer too! So it becomes a bit quicker later on where you must know the commands and how to crack the security of various systems as the game progresses while fighting a clock too. You should pick up these skills as you play, but the knowledge of how to access certain databases will require a bit more thought at times. This is where the game adds a bit of strategy and puzzling into the mix. You need to think about what you are trying to do, search through maybe several other computers not just tools, but possibly passwords to OTHER computers, and even find ways to crack encrypted files! So it isn't always completely straightforward with the game holding your hand to get what you need. You will absolutely need to think somewhat critically here to reach your goals. IT is very refreshing to find a game that doesn't just offer you solutions on a silver platter and challenges you to figure things out yourself. It is quite rewarding in some cases to find a solution after thinking all your options through. Sometimes you can even find solutions to future problems by just HACKING into things you aren't even supposed to be working on for no other reason than because you felt like it. 

Hacknet had a few bugs when I got it at release, but it appears that most have been taken care of. I finished the game, but I had a quest that didn't trigger properly so I had to hack my way around into other things to find the info I needed to proceed. Something that really wasn't that big a deal because it felt like I was actually doing something I figured out myself to get around a problem. The triggers have been patched now though as far as I know. Other than that nothing I ran into. 

Hacknet does make you feel like a hacker if you have never done any hacking before in your life. It does use real world terminology and command lines to satisfy those that have in the past too so it isn't just for the hacker n00bs out there. The fast paced and tech-y music playing in the background was designed to make you feel like you are hacking systems as a hero in a movie. Punching in commands as fast you can can before getting caught is definitely helped by the pace of the music playing while you are trying to look into the dirty secrets of every computer you hack into. 

I found Hacknet to be a fantastic feeling of hacking and mystery solving. While you may feel that the middle gets a little bit repetitive when it comes to the hacking, it does usually change up enough in what you need to use to keep the pacing OK. Usually what you find in the files, and of course the ending was payoff enough to continue through if you start to feel like you are staring at a flashing screen too long. I absolutely would not recommend this game to a casual gamer at all. Unlike say a point and click adventure, the puzzles you solve here will require quick thinking and quick fingers at times. Most players will be fine with this, but this is a game that require MUCH more activity on the keyboard than it does with a mouse. So you are typing commands for what you need to do in, and not using a mouse to solve puzzles as much. If you don't read the help files, the tutorial, and look at the academic databases in the game you will not be able to figure things out. If you want a brainless game this one is not for you.

The game has trading cards of course and Steam Achievements, which should be fairly easy to 100% if you can get through the game. This game should take you anywhere from 5-10 hours. More if you look ar ound some and find every secret I suspect.

NOTE: Something I didn't talk about, because I am unsure what it consists of, is that Hacknet will be releasing a patch at some point that includes not just Steam Workshop to add more player made "questing", but it will also have Multiplayer! Like I said I don't know much about those aspects, but they are definitely coming. MP was in the game before Steam so it already exists, but the developers didn't feel it was working well enough yet to release with the Steam release. They wanted to stamp out any single player bugs first before bringing in these other features.

The triggers have been patched now though as far as I know. Other than that nothing I ran into. Hacknet does make you feel like a hacker if you have never done any hacking before in your life. It does use real world terminology and command lines to satisfy those that have in the past too so it isn't just for the hacker n00bs out there. The fast paced and tech-y music playing in the background was designed to make you feel like you are hacking systems as a hero in a movie. Punching in commands as fast you can can before getting caught is definitely helped by the pace of the music playing while you are trying to look into the dirty secrets of every computer you hack into. I found Hacknet to be a fantastic feeling of hacking and mystery solving. While you may feel that the middle gets a little bit repetitive when it comes to the hacking, it does usually change up enough in what you need to use to keep the pacing OK. Usually what you find in the files, and of course the ending was payoff enough to continue through if you start to feel like you are staring at a flashing screen too long. I absolutely would not recommend this game to a casual gamer at all. Unlike say a point and click adventure, the puzzles you solve here will require quick thinking and quick fingers at times. Most players will be fine with this, but this is a game that require MUCH more activity on the keyboard than it does with a mouse. So you are typing commands for what you need to do in, and not using a mouse to solve puzzles as much. If you don't read the help files, the tutorial, and look at the academic databases in the game you will not be able to figure things out. If you want a brainless game this one is not for you. The game has trading cards of course and Steam Achievements, which should be fairly easy to 100% if you can get through the game. This game should take you anywhere from 5-10 hours. More if you look ar ound some and find every secret I suspect. NOTE: Something I didn't talk about, because I am unsure what it consists of, is that Hacknet will be releasing a patch at some point that includes not just Steam Workshop to add more player made "questing", but it will also have Multiplayer! Like I said I don't know much about those aspects, but they are definitely coming. MP was in the game before Steam so it already exists, but the developers didn't feel it was working well enough yet to release with the Steam release. They wanted to stamp out any single player bugs first before bringing in these other features.

This may be the biggest "fear" new players may have after viewing the trailer. This game involves typing out commands in a terminal, but really it's just similar to a "text based" adventure with commands. If you're new to using a CMD line (terminal) this is a perfect engaging way to become more familiar with how it works. Just like any new game once you get familiar with the controls you'll breeze through it. No spoilers. I can say that there is a story and that you will be highly involved with in. There is a lot of mysteries, and plenty of interesting characters to learn about. I should mention that each new play through of the game will have many events randomized. In addition the story continues in the DLC and that I found it totally worth it.

4. Final Thoughts
It's good. I personally had some doubts but once I started playing I couldn't stop. I wouldn't be leaving a review if I didn't think it deserved more attention.

TL;DR - Be the best Hackerman you can be just for a few bucks. Don't missout and be a scriptkiddie like Newman on Jurassic Park, a dinosaur ate his face...don't let a dinosaur eat your face.

***UPDATE - I finally played the DLC "Labyrinths" and damn, Picking it it up is a must if your gonna play this game. It opens up so much more and shows you easily what a Hacknet 2 could be.

After playing a game like Mainlining, I felt i had a love for a new genre of game but that game specifically just didn't satisfy me enough, it was wayyy to easy. I needed to know what the next level up from there was. After looking around a bit I found several other Hacker-esk types of games but only 2 specifically called out to me, Uplink and Hacknet. While it seems definitively that Uplink is the top dog in this genres arena, I gotta admit i didn't want to step into something that might be too overwhelming for me, so I went with Hacknet; the game people say is its spiritual sequel.

Having played this game now on my 3rd play through 35hrs in(pre dlc) i gotta say i think im in love. This game just feels right in a lot of places as to what you would want from a game like this.

The story while Is short and leaves some questions unanswered. It definitely makes you feel like you are part of its world for the most part. The fact that the world is open enough to have hidden crevices/coves of information to find behind hacked emails and encrypted documents, well outside of whatever story or mission you are focused on is more than enough to feel like this is a fun sandbox to play in.

The Interface is pretty much the only graphics you get but even so it does the job. And since you can change the theme/layout later in the game, the preference is on you, they all look great to me though.

The Music is amazing (some of it feels as good as a Hotline Miami soundtrack), it's sometimes perfectly in the foreground at times syncing to what you have to deal with at the moment and other times its just softly in the background letting you focus on what you need to do next.

This game is so simple but ingenious once you dive into it. I would recommend anyone that don't mind a bit of reading and some critical thinking puzzles pick this up.

You are a hacker that has found yourself in the middle of some hacking factions that may have stumbled into something big. Just like everything in the hacking community, all useful information is hidden on systems which need to be hacked into. While looking for that information you will uncover many more secrets as you figure out exactly what happened. A final ending that could be considered a "shock". They have made it easier for you by allowing you to hit "TAB" in certain places to have the game auto-complete command lines if there is nothing else that has the exact same characters and you are in the proper place to do so, however. It absolutely helps to have some typing speed, or at least the knowledge of where all the keys on the keyboard are without having to search them out all the time though. You will have issues if you are THAT slow.

Some computers early on are very easy to hack with only having to open 1-2 ports, but as you find more tools you may have to open as many as 5 ports, break through a firewall, and get through a proxy all on the same PC while avoiding a tracer too! So it becomes a bit quicker later on where you must know the commands and how to crack the security of various systems as the game progresses while fighting a clock too. You should pick up these skills as you play, but the knowledge of how to access certain databases will require a bit more thought at times. This is where the game adds a bit of strategy and puzzling into the mix. You need to think about what you are trying to do, search through maybe several other computers not just tools, but possibly passwords to OTHER computers, and even find ways to crack encrypted files! Like I said I don't know much about those aspects, but they are definitely coming. MP was in the game before Steam so it already exists, but the developers didn't feel it was working well enough yet to release with the Steam release. They wanted to stamp out any single player bugs first before bringing in these other features.

review_text_raw:
Hacknet is a fantastic hacking game with an interesting story. The interface is built around a set of simulated command line tools very close to the real Unix environment which is generally easy to use although the game map can get crowded in the late stages of the game. The atmosphere really does create the impression of being a hacker finding a target system's weaknesses, digging through your target's files and investigating what your contracts require. The gameplay rewards exploration and the game itself is peppered with lots of flourishes and attention to detail that really shows the love and effort put in by the developers. It recreates everything from private conversations to stupid corporate communications and IT practices (and even in-game OS crashes) realistically which makes for a very authentic game world.

While there are occasional typos and part of the gameplay loop migh seem repetitive, the flow of the game is very addictive and many times what starts off as a short session ends up taking up several hours. The game can definitely be enjoyed by non-computer savvy users although those with command-line experience are sure to find some amusing little touches that enhance the overall experience. The music and visuals are also very pleasant.

All in all, highly recommended and looking forward to playing the expansion!

review_text_raw:
A highly immersive game given how graphically simple it is: basically just a bunch of text and menus. The world-building makes you really feel like a hacker being hired by various people to do all sorts of tasks. I enjoyed the game more than a lot of far more visually impressive games.

I must stress that the 'hacking' part is vastly simplified. It barely touches the basics of hacking, so don't expect the game to teach you how to hack in real-life, though it might just inspire you to learn it properly yourself. The technical aspect of the gameplay also starts to get repetitive once you've tried out all the commands and programs available to you, somewhere around the half-way point. However, the real thrill and challenge of the game lies in digging up useful information and files in the various devices you hack into, analyse them and then figure out how you can use them in order to accomplish your goal. In a sense, this feels like a hacking-themed detective game. There's also a story to the game that really picks up near the end, though some might find it a bit vague at parts.

While I thoroughly enjoyed the game from start to finish, I have to say that this game isn't for everyone. First of all, you gotta be prepared to read a lot. You don't have to read all the text, as many of the text files are purely comedic in nature, having nothing to do with accomplishing the task at hand and are just there to entertain you, but on the other hand, there are a lot of them that contain vital information towards completing your task, even if you don't realise it at first. You definitely need to be patient and observant if you want to beat the game on your own, as well as having good deductive skills to put the information you find to good use. The game does make you think a bit, though not to the extent of typical puzzle games. There are also educational text files that teach you how the various commands and programs in the game work. If you enjoy reading, then I'm sure you would enjoy this game, though there are a few typos here and there that can be annoying.

As for the gameplay, when you're not reading stuff, you're pretty much just typing away commands on your keyboard or just clicking buttons that appear on screen on the UI with your mouse. You don't have to type out everything in full, as you can use the Tab key to auto-complete commands and file names, but it does help to have good typing skills, especially as there are quite a few timed challenges in the game.

All in all, Hacknet does a great job as a hacking simulator game, making you feel like an actual hacker while still being fun to play, even if the hacking aspect is significantly dumbed-down. I recommend this game to those who wish to experience what it's like to be one of those hackers you often see in movies without having to deal with the high technical difficulty of actual hacking. Experienced hackers might find it too simple to be enjoyable, though.

review_text_raw:
I’ve never hacked real computer systems (or anything for that matter), so take this statement with a grain of salt. Hacknet made me feel like a real hacker. A good game should be fun and immersive. Hacknet aces both of those criteria. The story starts you off getting an email from a hacker named ‘Bit’ who confesses to already being dead and needing your help to stop something horrible from coming.

The game does a good job of introducing itself. The mechanic is based mostly in a terminal prompt with a retro-esque UI. The number of commands that you need to remember are minimal thankfully and most of the navigating to do routine tasks can be done by simply clicking. However, if you’re looking for a purer feeling everything can be done purely from command line. The parts of the game that require breaking into a computer system do require use of the command line for the most part.

Once you have the basics of breaking into a system down, the game then raises the difficulty by introducing a system where you are traced by the system you are trying to break into. While the steps of hacking don’t change much as the game progresses, the game does make sure to include new challenges. Make sure you have pen and paper nearby, there is plenty you will need to write down. (Or take pictures with your phone like I did) As the game continues, the challenges become less about breaking into the system itself and more about following a trail of information to get what you need. This includes thinking about the information given rather than simply following instructions. 

I won’t say that the game is without flaw. In a few places what you need to do to complete a task takes more than just normal careful consideration. I am fully willing to accept lack of intelligence on my part as the excuse for this. 

In short, if you like puzzle games and you’re not put off by my description, then do give this game a chance. The experience is well worth the price.

Make sure you have pen and paper nearby, there is plenty you will need to write down. (Or take pictures with your phone like I did) As the game continues, the challenges become less about breaking into the system itself and more about following a trail of information to get what you need. This includes thinking about the information given rather than simply following instructions. I won’t say that the game is without flaw. In a few places what you need to do to complete a task takes more than just normal careful consideration. I am fully willing to accept lack of intelligence on my part as the excuse for this. In short, if you like puzzle games and you’re not put off by my description, then do give this game a chance. The experience is well worth the price.

Late review, but, just gonna say: Awesome game.

Great Soundtrack, Colorful UI, Amazing Mechanics and somewhat Touching Story.

I would say something about each part, but really, words can't exactly describe the neat feeling of Hacking to a beat from the likes of Remi Gallego, Carpenter Brut, Tonspender and much more.

Being a computer geek personally, I can verify the whole 'Based on real UNIX commands' thing is pretty spot on. Granted, it removes a few commands, but I am sure that can be passed on given the audience this is meant for (All.)

I highly recommend this game if you're a little tired of something like 'Uplink' for instance. Or if you just generally want to feel like a Hacker. It's really addicting.

9.8/10

Now, honestly, this sort of lacks a few things though, and they might be commonly shared things. Like... Upgrades, as one thing. It's understandable to not add Upgrades, since it would probably make the player OP. But really, it would be nice to get additional RAM throughout the game. I don't exactly care how, or why, it just seems like something that would be a good addition. Another thing could also be more Paths. This is a bit of a spoiler, so read off from this next bit if you haven't unlocked all the achievements or done everything possible:

So far, I only found 2 paths to go on. The first path being the goody-two-shoes, going with Entropy, and going through with the CSEC tests. The second path being tracking Naix, deleting his files, and then going on from his E-Mail to vandalize Nortron's servers, to get into the /el community (A really funny spoof to the likes of 4 Chan, 8Chan, or any particular Image Board that stays in the theme of Free-Speech.) and going on from there. Personally, I would love to see something like a 'Independant' path or a 'Brutal' path. Something like those I wish could be in this.

But, asides from all this though, again, really awesome game.

Side Note: Red Line. Have fun with that ;)
